summary: This proposed standard defines the notation used for conformance statements in SNMPv2, which describe the minimum a product must implement and what it actually implements. It was replaced by RFC 1904.

eli5.summary: This paper gives a way to write a checklist saying what a product has to do and what it actually does.

questions: how to describe mib implementation level
what is an object-group in a mib
how do mib conformance statements work
subtitle: Three notations for saying what a MIB module requires and what a given agent actually implements.

tldr.problem: A MIB module defines many objects, but implementors need a precise way to state the minimum that must be implemented and the level actually achieved.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines three macros: OBJECT-GROUP collects related objects, MODULE-COMPLIANCE states the minimum requirements, and AGENT-CAPABILITIES records what a specific agent supports and where it differs.
tldr.outcome: It was a Proposed Standard for SNMPv2 and has been replaced by RFC 1904.

today: RFC 1444 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 1904, which is the version to use.

sections.title: Why Conformance Statements
sections.content:
A network management system has agents on many nodes, at least one management station and a management protocol. Management information is a collection of managed objects stored in a virtual store called the Management Information Base (MIB), and related objects are defined in MIB modules written in the SMI, a subset of ASN.1.

The RFC says it may be useful to define the acceptable lower bound of an implementation along with the level actually achieved, and its purpose is to define the notation for both. For exposition it calls the original framework (RFCs 1155, 1157 and 1212) SNMPv1 and the current framework SNMPv2.
sections.eli5: People who build devices need a clear way to say how much of the rulebook they must follow and how much they really do.

sections.title: Grouping Objects with OBJECT-GROUP
sections.content:
The OBJECT-GROUP macro defines a conformance group, a collection of related managed objects. Its expansion conceptually happens during implementation, not at run time.

To implement an object, an agent must return a reasonably accurate value for retrieval and, if the object is writable, be able to influence the managed entity on a set. An agent that cannot implement an object must return an exception or error such as noSuchObject. It must never return a value for an object it does not implement.

The OBJECTS clause is required and names the objects, all defined in the same module, each with a MAX-ACCESS of read-only, read-write or read-create. STATUS is current or obsolete, and DESCRIPTION is required. The value of the macro is an OBJECT IDENTIFIER naming the group. The RFC's example groups the seven MIB-II system objects as systemGroup.
sections.eli5: A group is a labelled bag of related features. If you say you have the bag, every item in it has to be in there, and you must never pretend to have an item you do not.

sections.title: Stating Minimums with MODULE-COMPLIANCE
sections.content:
The MODULE-COMPLIANCE macro conveys the minimum implementation requirements for one or more MIB modules. Every standard MIB module needs a compliance specification, either in the same module or a companion one.

A MODULE clause names each module. MANDATORY-GROUPS lists the groups that must be implemented unconditionally: an agent that returns noSuchObject for any object in a mandatory group is not conformant. GROUP clauses name groups that are conditionally mandatory (for example, only if a protocol is implemented) or optional, and each needs a DESCRIPTION giving the conditions. A group named in neither clause is unconditionally optional.

An OBJECT clause refines the requirement for one object, with optional SYNTAX, WRITE-SYNTAX and MIN-ACCESS refinements. A compliant implementation provides access at least the minimum and at most the maximum set in the object definition. The RFC's example lets a system claim MIB-II compliance with only read access to tcpConnState.
sections.eli5: The compliance statement is the must-have list: these bags are required, these only if you have a certain part, and these are optional. It can also say that for one item, doing a little less is fine.

sections.title: Describing One Agent with AGENT-CAPABILITIES
sections.content:
The AGENT-CAPABILITIES macro lets an agent implementor describe the precise level of support claimed for a MIB group and bind that description to the agent's sysObjectID or to an snmpORID instance in the snmpORTable. A management station can keep a database of these statements, look up the agent's sysObjectID and optimize how it talks to that agent. It specifies variations relative to the OBJECT-TYPE definitions, not relative to compliance statements.

A PRODUCT-RELEASE clause describes the release. Each SUPPORTS clause names a MIB module and an INCLUDES list of groups. A VARIATION clause names an object implemented in a refined way, with optional SYNTAX, WRITE-SYNTAX, ACCESS (including not-implemented), CREATION-REQUIRES and DEFVAL, plus a required DESCRIPTION. The write-only access value exists only for backward compatibility and must not be used for new object types.

The RFC's usage example describes a 4BSD agent that supports MIB-II except the egp group, does not implement ipInAddrErrors, restricts the syntax of several objects and makes tcpConnState read-only.
sections.eli5: Where compliance is the must-have list, this is the sticker on one particular product: here is what this one has, and here is what is a bit different.

sections.title: Extending an Information Module
sections.content:
When an information module is revised, the rules in Section 10 of RFC 1442 apply, and this memo adds three. If any non-editorial change is made to a clause of an object group, a compliance definition or a capabilities definition, its OBJECT IDENTIFIER value must be changed, along with its descriptor.

The effect is that a given identifier always refers to exactly the same requirements.
sections.eli5: If you change what is in a labelled bag in any real way, it must get a new label, so nobody mixes up the old bag and the new one.

data.title: systemGroup
data.code:
systemGroup OBJECT-GROUP
    OBJECTS     { sysDescr, sysObjectID, sysUpTime,
                  sysContact, sysName, sysLocation,
                  sysServices }
    STATUS  current
    DESCRIPTION
            "The system group defines objects which are common
            to all managed systems."
    ::= { mibIIGroups 1 }
